title: Emotions high in tearful sentencing hearing for Kenneth Law, guilty in Ontario of 14 counts of aiding suicide

image.caption: Ashtyn Prosser-Blake is seen with his mother Kim and brother Drake in this photo on Kim Prosser's Facebook page. (Submitted by Kim Prossner)

blocks.text: Poison seller Kenneth Law pleads guilty to abetting 14 suicides

Poison seller Kenneth Law pleaded guilty to counselling or aiding 14 suicides in Ontario. Law has been tied to 147 other deaths worldwide, including the United Kingdom where he will not be prosecuted, triggering outrage from victims' families.

items: September 23'He should be here'The Crown read out the statement of Danielle, mother of Dylan Cerny-Salisbury. In it, she said his death shattered her life "into a million pieces."She said her family is not only grieving the life he lived, but the life he never had the opportunity to live."He mattered. He should be here," Danielle said.Dylan, who was 18 at the time of his death, had been diagnosed with anxiety, depression, ADHD, a mood disorder and borderline personality disorder. "His struggles were part of his story, but not his story," she said.She said he kept putting pieces of his life back together and moving forward but that his "future was taken from him."He was found in his room by his 14-year-old sister, who thought he was sleeping.

'Crushed my world'Mark GollomAshtyn Prosser-Blake is seen with his mother Kim and brother Drake in this photo on Kim Prosser's Facebook page. (Submitted by Kim Prossner)Kim Prosser, mother of Ashtyn Prosser-Blake, recalled the last phone call she had with her son.She recalled that she thought he was just tired, and didn't know he was making "his last phone call goodbye" before taking his life.Prosser broke down in tears, recounting her realization soon after that call, that "he's gone. Ashtyn is gone. [It] crushed my world."Prosser-Blake lived in the basement of his grandparents' home in Thunder Bay, Ont.When his grandmother went to check if the doors to the home were locked for the night, she found a journal at the top of the stairs saying, "goodbye."She went downstairs and found Ashtyn unresponsive. He was later declared dead at the hospital.

Aunt says her life was changed foreverMichelle Song The Crown read out the statement of Corrine King, aunt of Clayton Choquette."Our lives have changed forever" since Choquette died, her statement reads."As his aunt it is extremely difficult to accept someone we loved deeply is gone."King said that her family is left wondering what Choquette's life would have become if he hadn't died at just 32 years old. She said there will always be an empty place within their family. Choquette was found dead in his vehicle, after a bystander called authorities in August 2022.

'Numbness and anxiety'Mark GollomThe stepfather of Tyler Bryson told court that until Law is incarcerated, the emotional burden of his stepson's death remains enormous.He said he can't adequately explain how his death affected him, only that it's a combination of "numbness and anxiety."He said Tyler treated him like his own father and spoke about his time as a pilot, and his professionalism in his career.Tyler was found dead at the age of 34, in a rental car on May 2, 2023 near Toronto's BMO Field.Bryson had left instructions for first responders on how to ventilate the car and made a donation to charity for trauma to first responders in advance of his death.His stepfather said his stepson deserved support from a professional and didn't deserve to be "preyed upon" by Law.

Law sent over 1,200 packages to 41 countriesThomas DaigleThe deaths of (from top left) Neha Raju, Michael Dunham, Tom Parfett, Tom Windsor, Anthony Jones and Noelle Ramirez are all linked to Kenneth Law's companies. (muchloved.com; Devon Mind; submitted)While today's victim impact statements have so far focused on Kenneth Law's victims in Ontario, let's take a moment to underline the scale of suffering around the world linked to his actions.According to an agreed statement of facts, Law sent 1,209 packages to 41 countries, including 157 shipments to Canadian addresses and 431 shipments to the U.S.Authorities have linked Law's products to suicides in Ireland, Italy, New Zealand and beyond.The total number of deaths will most likely never be known, as not all suicides were investigated. In some cases, Law asked buyers of his poison to destroy evidence.Many families who lost loved ones will never get a chance to express their grief in court.

'Lost a piece of my soul,' mother saysMark GollomThe mother of victim Amara Scott (pictured) delivered her victim impact statement in court today. (Submitted by New Haven Funeral Centre)Sandra Scott, the mother of Amara Scott, said she's no longer the same person — that she was a mother of three, and is "now a mother of two.""[I have] lost a piece of my soul," she said.She broke down as she said it was an honour to be Amara's mother.Sandra Scott said she called police for a wellbeing check in 2022, when she did not show up for work. Amara was found deceased in her apartment in Toronto.

'Losing Stephen changed my sense of safety'Michelle Song Latha Mitchell, the stepmother of Stephen Mitchell, sobbed as she delivered her statement."Losing Stephen changed my sense of safety and the way I looked at the world," she said.Latha shared the toll her stepson's death had on herself, her husband and other family members.She says she experienced many "sleepless nights" thinking of him. Her husband, she says, became withdrawn and struggled to focus at work, ultimately losing his job.Latha says the loss of Stephen could never be filled by anyone or anything.Other members of the family wept with her. When she returned to her seat after finishing her statement, she was greeted by her husband with a hug.

Father will remain vigilant of Law post-releaseMark GollomThe Poison Seller | Documentary TrailerComing soon on CBC Gem and CBC Television. Exclusive recordings and shocking new revelations expose the untold story behind the Kenneth Law case, the Canadian investigation that captured global attention.The father of Stephen Mitchell said when Law is released from prison, he will remain vigilant should he ever attempt to again sell the products that led to the death of his victims.Stephen Mitchell Sr.'s son suffered from depression and had stopped taking his anti-depressant medication. The 21-year-old was found dead by his brother in his bed in their family home in Toronto in March 2023.Mitchell Sr. said he believes Law has had feelings of regret, or that life was meaningless, while in custody — the same thoughts he said his son must have felt.While Law may regain his freedom, it will "never erase the consequences of what you have done," Mitchell Sr. said.An upcoming documentary on Kenneth Law will focus on victims' families around the world, including the Mitchells. The Poison Seller will be available on CBC Gem on Sept. 28.
Law shows no responseMark GollomAs the first impact statements were read into court, Law sat in the prisoner's box, blankly staring ahead.He has shown no response or emotion.

Emotions highMichelle Song The sounds of sniffles have started to fill the background of the courtroom, as victims' families started getting emotional after hearing impact statements from other families.Some reached for tissues, wiping away tears. One woman held her head down, buried in her hands.
